title: The smuggler
hookLine: for years a border guard searches his saddlebags and finds nothing, because he was smuggling donkeys (Nasruddin tale)
last: LET THOSE WHO KNOW TELL THE OTHERS.

cards: Ever hunted the whole house for your glasses while they sat on your head? Or searched for your phone using its own flashlight? The thing you're missing is often the thing you're holding.

Today, a border guard with that problem, for years. Every week, a man comes across the frontier leading a donkey loaded with bundles of straw. And every week the guard is sure he's smuggling something.
He can see it in the man's face, in his new clothes, in his growing house. The man is Nasruddin.

teach.b: The guard does everything right. He unties the bundles and shakes out every stalk. He checks the saddlebags, pats Nasruddin down, looks in his shoes, sometimes even burns the straw to see if something's hidden in it.
Nothing. Week after week, nothing, and week after week, Nasruddin gets richer. Years pass.
Both men grow old. The guard retires, and one day, in another town, he spots Nasruddin in a teahouse and sits down beside him. Please, he says, I'm not a guard anymore.
What were you smuggling? Nasruddin sips his tea: donkeys. That's the whole secret.

teach.h: HE NEVER LOOKED AT THE DONKEY.
teach.b: The guard was so busy searching what the donkey carried that he never looked at the donkey, walking past him every week, in plain sight, the whole point. We do the same: search the details, miss the obvious.
A worried parent checks every homework answer and misses that the child is sad.
A company counts every expense and misses that its best people are leaving. You look for what's wrong in a friendship and miss that you haven't called in months. Now look back at the week.
Nasruddin searched under the lamp because the light was better. He fed soup to his coat. He rode backward.
He told everyone they were right. His pot gave birth and died. He never gave the sermon.
And today, he walked the answer right past the guard. Seven stories, one teacher, and each time the lesson was in plain sight, disguised as a joke.

how: The smuggler is one of the Nasruddin tales most often retold in teaching and business talks as a picture of missing the obvious; in Iran and Central Asia he is usually called Mulla Nasruddin, in Turkey Nasreddin Hoca.

o: a guard who searched every load at the border
a thief hiding gold inside bundles of straw
Nasruddin, slipping donkeys past a guard for years

s: he never did. he only learned the answer years later, retired, over tea.
the thing crossing the border was the animal the guard never looked at.
this week's stories all came from one written book
they belong to Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim folk tradition, and versions vary from town to town.

games.q: you're the guard. for years you've searched every bundle and found nothing, yet the man grows rich. where haven't you looked?
games.why: years later he asks, and Nasruddin says: donkeys. the answer walked past him every week, in plain sight.

practice: Think of a problem you've been searching hard, stalk by stalk through the straw. Now step back and look at the whole donkey: what walks right past you every week that you've stopped noticing, a tiredness, a person, a habit, a gift?
Don't solve it; just name it quietly, once.

wordCard.voice: The smuggler. A guard searches the straw for years, and never sees that the thing crossing the border is the donkey. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, mulla: a learned man. In Iran and Central Asia he is Mulla Nasruddin.

carryVoice: Your line: it's the donkey. The answer was never in the straw. That's Nasruddin's week.
